content.overview: Cannabis inflorescences and glandular trichomes do not mature perfectly synchronously. Harvest decisions become more defensible when they sample multiple representative sites and preserve cultivar, plant position and age context.

vocabulary.definition: A sample selected to reflect meaningful variation in the larger lot or crop.
Systematic distortion caused by selecting observations that do not represent the target population.
Variation in developmental state among flowers, trichomes or canopy positions.

sections.title: One flower is not the crop
sections.body: Trichome development varies with plant age and genotype and can be asynchronous within inflorescences, so a single viewed site cannot establish a universal maturity percentage.

sections.title: Sampling position matters
sections.body: Canopy light, architecture and flower age can create spatial differences. Record plant and flower position when comparing maturity observations.

sections.title: Harvest criteria should be explicit
sections.body: Define what evidence is being observed, how many sites are sampled and how the result connects to the production objective rather than relying on a universal color rule.

workedExamples: If upper flowers appear more mature than interior flowers, sample both positions before characterizing the whole crop.
Two cultivars at the same calendar day may not share the same trichome-development pattern.
commonMistakes: Using one microscope field as lot evidence.
Treating a trichome color percentage as universally valid.
content.practicalApplication: Create a maturity sampling map covering multiple plants and flower positions, and record cultivar, date, developmental observations and the harvest decision criterion.
content.summary: Maturity assessment is a sampling problem as well as a biological observation.
